utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may very briefly, not to use up any unnecessary time, we have been informed that the witness, if possible, needs to leave The Hague tomorrow for his own ongoing business, which is important and critical. Therefore, in order to make -- try to make that possible we would ask if we could sit today with shorter breaks, 20 minute breaks, and if we could sit for a longer period till -- perhaps till 7.30. By our calculation we have used approximately 237 minutes with this witness. We anticipate using another ten minutes. If we sit the extra time as we've proposed, that will be 275 minutes which leaves -- which means in that time we could -- the Defence could have as long as the Prosecution had for its cross and that would leave approximately 20 to 30 minutes for questions from the Bench and any redirect examination. I understand that it may not work but if we could try to make it happen, we would be grateful and I'm sure Mr. Kirudja will be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When were you told that the witness has to leave tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This morning, Your Honour. We have been under the -- I had had the understanding and Ms. Richterova had the understanding that he could stay until Saturday, and it's my understanding that the witness is here, he can speak to it if necessary, my understanding that if it's absolutely -- if he has to be here tomorrow, then he'll be here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Mr. Milovancevic, very briefly, do you have anything to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We are quite taken aback by this proposal. There were no indications that we would have to face such a situation. The OTP foresaw the conclusion of their cross-examination during that second session. Therefore, they miscalculated. What is of essence for us is that this is an exceptionally important witness for us. This witness was there in the material time and in the area discussed in the indictment, and we haven't had a witness who was in position of such great knowledge about the relevant events. This request to sit longer today would mean that our breaks are shortened in between sessions, and this is no longer on the basis of equal footing as regards this question -- this witness's examination. The conditions that the OTP enjoyed are not the same when it came to the Defence, then. They had a lot of time at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand how shorter breaks make it not -- make the footing unequal. However, and I do take your point that, yes, the Prosecution took longer than they said they were going to take with this witness. But the Prosecution is not alone in this mistake. The Defence is also partly to blame. You'll remember that at the beginning of the testimony of this witness, and I know I was not here but I read the record, Ms. Richterova did apologise to the witness for having kept him waiting for so long. And that was because of the cross-examination that took place of the previous witness, and I did talk about it when that cross-examination was taking place, Mr. Milovancevic. It is of the utmost important that we complete with this witness and I do not want to us waste more time debating this issue. I would like us to get to the solution of the problem as soon as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the examination is always conducted in the presence of the entire Chamber. In this situation we cannot be held accountable for anything that has occurred. It is non-existence when it comes to our guilt. We don't need additional 20 minutes at the expense of our breaks. I would like to thank you for having granted that, but we will just do with whatever time we have on our hands. But I just wanted to have it for the record that just before we are supposed to start a cross-examination, conditions change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Okay. Then the Chamber is going to rule as follows: That we will try to accommodate the witness as much as we possibly can today. And this is dependent on whether everybody else is available. When I say everybody else I'm talking about the technicians, I'm talking about the interpreters, and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Assuming that everybody -- before I make. Let me not make an assumption. Let me just check with everybody, the people from registry, people from interpretation, people from the technicians and the AVS, if we try to sit longer, would that be okay? Interpreters? I'm being advised that's okay. Okay, then we are going to sit like this, then. We will sit up to 1545 today and at 1545 we will take a break up to 1605. That will be a 20 minute break. We will reconvene at 1605 and sit until 1735. We will then break at 1735 until 1755, and at 1755 we will sit up until 1925 or 1930, no longer than that. Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Kirudja, you may very well remember but notwithstanding that, it is still my duty to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start, I want to move into evidence 65 ter Exhibit 887, which we discussed before the break yesterday and I didn't manage to move it officially into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit 65 ter 887 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 764, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, yesterday we moved into the year 1994. I would like to ask you, during 1993, 1994, did you participate or observe any negotiations between Croatia and Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a lengthy process that we participated in, from the ground in the Krajina, and to outside the country where the negotiations took us, into Geneva and Vienna and back. I participated in that entire process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you at this stage? I think in the interests of time, I'll ask you, Mr. Kirudja, to please listen carefully to the questions and answer -- sufficiently to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't give long explanations that are not necessary. Control your witness, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Without going into too many details based on your observations, what was Mr. Martic's attitude towards these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not involved directly in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was all these negotiations without his participations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether he was able, out of his position as president, involved the results of any negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end the negotiations were structured in such a way that towards the end, the leaders in Knin were being brought into the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And towards the end, what was their attitude towards these negotiations? Were any agreements successful?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Successfully reached? And what was the reason why not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to put the exact wording to it but from one side, they looked like they were going to be successful, and from the Serb side, they looked like they were not successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was this -- I'm bearing in mind the comment of Their Honours not to go into long explanation. I don't know how to make you understand that we -- the negotiations were structured in a certain way to reach a certain conclusion, and when that conclusion seemed to be achieved, then once -- Serb side seems to be kind of getting cold feet, and not wishing to proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to show the witness document -- it's not 65 ter, it's ERN number is R 00311012. Before this document is displayed, you already told us that at certain point of time in 1994, you were assigned to a certain position in Belgrade; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the position you were in?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two titles, which were -- the first title was the delegate of the special representative of the Secretary-General where I had political responsibilities, reporting directly to the SRSG in Belgrade and in Montenegro; Podgorica, responsibilities there. The second title I kept from the field, I was also the coordinator of civil affairs, CAC. I had those two titles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think we do not have exactly the page. It should be -- the last four digits would be 1012. Ah, wonderful. Did this position bring you to attend certain meetings in which Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Martic would be present?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at this document? It's dated 24 of November, and it says meeting in Belgrade with president Milosevic and Mr. Martic. Were you present during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the date on the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The date of the meeting was from the text of paragraph 1, it says yesterday, and because this document is dated 24th of November, it was 23rd of November.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The document itself also indicates I was in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you were -- were you able to go through this document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the entirety of this document? Can you scroll down on it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we please scroll down? And we can also move to other pages.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you reviewed this document, is this an accurate record of the meeting in which you participated?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what did you observe, if anything, during this meeting, about the relationship between Mr. Martic and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of this document centre around air strikes in an airport called Udbina. NATO had struck that airport. There were a lot of intense feelings about this action of NATO from the Serb side. There was, of course, high concern about the actions of the Serbs that led to NATO taking this action, and the force commander at that time, Delaprel, was also concerned about those incidents. The discussion, therefore, was kind of tense on that regard, with Mr. Akashi trying to get certain clarifications about the events leading to the air strikes, and the consequences of that air strike. Mr. Milosevic, trying also to provide some understanding between what happened and what the UN, led by Mr. Akashi, was saying, that was basically the situation where Mr. Milosevic was trying to iron out what seemed to be lack of understanding of events leading to the strike and after the strike, between the UN on the one side and Mr. Martic on the other side, who was responsible for those forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, can we now focus on relationship between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Martic, as you observed either during this meeting or any time before or any time after? What was the evolution of their relationship, as you observed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the number of meetings I had with Mr. Milosevic, not all of which Mr. Martic was in - some he was not - and also where he was, the relationship at the early part was Milosevic trying to achieve a certain end, a certain outcome, with regard to this area that was called Republic of Serbian Krajina. Specifically and in very short description, it was his vision that it could be negotiated into an autonomous region within Croatia. He seemed very carefully to guide this outcome and each time something that happened from the ground, that seemed not consistent with that view, he would try to guide Mr. Martic towards that goal. This worked for some time, until a certain point, they parted company because Mr. Milosevic and -- would expect certain results, actions would be taken on the ground which negated those results, and at a certain point they parted company.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 765, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Kirudja, please listen carefully what the question is asking for and answer what the question says.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I remind you also, Mr. Milovancevic, to control your witness, to ask very concise questions and just elicit answers without giving speeches before you ask questions. We are going to watch the time. It is now 1438, I think. And you are warned, Mr. Milovancevic, that you will be kept strictly to the time that the Prosecution took to examine this witness. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the warning, Your Honour. I have understood this but I would like to note that a witness who was at such a position and who is so educated, we have not had so far, and there is no other on the Prosecutor's list. What the witness can tell us about the Vance Plan and what happened on the ground during that period is so significant that I might even want to go beyond the allocated time, but I hope it will be justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, good afternoon. I'm Predrag Milovancevic, Defence counsel for Mr. Martic. You are probably aware that we are about to start your cross-examination. Given your educational background, given you're long experience in the United Nations, and your long presence in the entire territory that is covered by the indictment, I'm going to ask you a number of questions. I am grateful for your patience and I would like to thank you in advance for your cooperation. I would also like to draw your attention to the honourable Judge Moloto's words about the efficiency of our work. The basis of your arrival in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Kirudja, was the so-called Vance Plan. You've explained to the Honourable Judges that the plan envisaged a peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia. Am I right in saying that this plan envisaged two components, a military component and a civilian component. The military component was to be composed of the 10.000 UNPROFOR soldiers who had infantry weaponry, armoured vehicles, helicopters and a civilian police, some 500 monitors in all, and the total of these men was around 10.000? Am I right in thinking that and in saying that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes. The mission was composed of the elements you have named. The numbers are not readily clear -- I can't remember readily whether there were 10.000 or below 10.000 but the components are as you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are talking about the Vance Plan, this has already been admitted into evidence by the Prosecutor during your examination-in-chief, its basic principles, and especially its general principles, did they envisage for the peacekeeping operation of the United Nations in Yugoslavia should provide for the conditions of peace and security that would be conducive to the negotiations leading to the solution of the Yugoslav crisis, without any prejudice to the possible outcome of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this commitment on the part of the peacekeeping operation, not to prejudice the possible outcome of these negotiations, did it exclude the possibility for certain members of the UNPROFOR or UNCIVPOL expect a certain outcome or even participate in the actions that would lead to a certain outcome? When I say that, I would also like to say that I condemn any such behaviour, of course, if we start from the assumption that such behaviour was indeed present.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your question is a bit difficult for me to extricate. I don't know what you mean, exclude certain members of UNPROFOR and UNCIVPOL from certain outcome. I don't understand that aspect of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Kirudja, if the question was not clear. This is what I meant. Such a mission of the United Nations peacekeeping mission, did it call for a complete neutrality of the personnel, and did it call only for one thing, and that was restoring and keeping peace and creating such conditions that would be conducive to negotiations with a view to resolving the crises in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With one more condition you have left out. Not only the conditions conducive to restoring peace, but also conducive for the people who were either internally displaced or forced out of that region to return voluntarily into the area. That was a written condition of the Vance Plan, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. I completely agree with what you have just said and this is exactly what I myself know about the Vance Plan. Is it correct that the provision of the Vance Plan on the deployment and functions of the peacekeeping forces of the United Nations envisaged a function of the protection of all the inhabitants of UNPA areas from attack and that -- and that was the role of the military component? On the other hand the role of the civilian component was to control the civilian police, the local police, that is, and making sure that they behaved in the same manner towards all the inhabitants of the area across the board?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. There are two parts of your question I shall respond to. The first one, that is peacekeeping forces of the UN being expected to protect all the inhabitants of the UNPA areas from attack. That is not quite what you may have implied. It was meant that all the armed elements in the sector would lay down their arms; therefore there would be no need for a fighting force of the UN or otherwise to achieve that protection. The burden of that protection was in all the combatants laying down their arms. Secondly on the question of that the UN behaved in certain manner, yes, the UN personnel, whether they are military or civil police, are indeed required to uphold a certain conduct, among which neutrality is that. But neutrality in certain meaning only, not an absolute neutrality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All the components of the peacekeeping operation of the United Nations, both the civilian and the military one, in keeping with the Vance Plan were supposed to be deployed in those areas in Croatia for which the Secretary-General deemed that they required special conditions in order to provide for a permanent cease-fire and for such a cease-fire with respect to all human rights and the control of the situation on the ground, to be conducive to negotiations that would lead towards a peaceful solution of the crisis. Would that be correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about these special areas which were to become areas under the UN protection, are we talking about those areas in which the Serbs were either a majority or a significant minority, and where tensions eventually resulted in armed conflict in the recent past?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had named areas where the conflict had already taken place by the time we arrived. Your question has an implication of things before we arrived. No, the areas where we were to be deployed were where the conflict had already taken place. Secondly, the Serbs were not -- there was no concept of minority or majority, because, as you yourself have explained earlier, the objective was to return the situation into a normal situation while a political solution is being negotiated elsewhere. Included in that expectation is the return of those people who already had been expelled by the time we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. In answering my learned friend's questions, you explained what the three United Nations areas were. You also gave us a list of the municipalities so we will not dwell upon that. However, with regard to the structure of the United Nations forces, can you confirm that in addition to the military forces and the civilian observers, the United Nations forces also included a group of military observers who were not armed and who were supposed to monitor the demilitarisation of these areas?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct and I regret that yesterday I forgot to mention them. Yes, the military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Vance Plan. As a plan that was drafted by the late Cyrus Vance, was the Vance Plan something that envisaged for the military and civilian members of the United Nations would be deployed when the Security Council decided to send its forces to the three areas of the former Yugoslavia? In order to avoid any confusion, in other words, when the Security Council deemed that the conditions were put in place for the personnel to be deployed, i.e., when there was a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to assure you that all the personnel, military, formed contingents, military observers, and civil police are authorised by the Security Council before they can be deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. When the Security Council of the United Nations passed the decision for the United Nations troops to be sent on a mission in the former Yugoslavia, was the process of the deployment of those forces and the taking over of the three areas under the protection of the United Nations in order to protect those areas? Was it synchronised and coordinated with the commanders of the forces of those JNA units which were on the ground at the time of the deployment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces that were deployed in the areas, all areas specifically areas in Sector North, were of course synchronised in terms of where they were to be deployed with the JNA forces, but not all the forces arrived at the same time. Some arrived at different times. So the synchronisation had a time line to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is absolutely clear. Thank you very much. My question was, relative to General Spiro Nikovic whom you mentioned in the best of light as the commander of the 10th Corps of the JNA, based in Bihac, outside of your sector, that is, and who had a number of meetings with yourself, negotiating the surrender of the area that was supposed to be taken over by the United Nations troops. In connection with this general, and I suppose the situation was the same or similar elsewhere, my question is as follows: Do you remember that the Vance Plan comprised a provision stipulating that the schedule for the deployment -- for the dislocation of the JNA troops would be agreed between the secretary of Defence of Yugoslavia and the -- you, the United Nations mission? Do you remember such a provision in the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The provision in the Vance Plan for the deployment, yes. The part about an agreement between the secretary of Defence of Yugoslavia and the UN mission, I wouldn't have a reason to be part of that because that was the force commander and the department at much higher level than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. I just quoted the provision of Article 18 of the basic principles under the title, "The dislocation of the JNA." We could open the document but I would rather not waste the Honourable Chamber's time. With regard to your last question, you've explained and you also stated in your statement to the OTP, that General Spiro Nikovic as commander of the JNA forces in the area explained that he had maps with the exact deployment of units and when they are supposed to withdraw, and that he was awaiting instructions from Belgrade. What General Nikovic did, does it seem to you like an action of an officer who is acting on the order of a higher authority or an action of a general who is acting independently of his own will?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remember that General Nikovic was a three-star general. He himself was a high authority in the military structure. They don't come higher except when you go to the fourth star general. Secondly, General Nikovic was reasonably familiar with the Vance Plan. When a general is given a task, he is given the results and it is left to him to achieve those results. He struck me as a person who was exactly doing that and also with a lot of discretion about the tactical way he goes about getting the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. I suppose that you remember the statement that you provided to my learned friends from the OTP and the part in which you described that at one of the first meetings that you had with General Nikovic, the JNA general, he told you that he wanted to hand over the area to which the UN, United Nations, troops were to be deployed, to hand it over in a good order, militarily and administratively. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very clearly. He called it, I want a clean situation when I hand over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. As regards the obligation of the demilitarisation of these three areas where the UN troops were to be deployed, it was envisaged that the JNA, once the UN troops were deployed, should withdraw from the entire area. Not only from the three protected areas but from the entire territory of the former Republic of Croatia. There is a report to the Security Council of the United Nations by the Secretary-General that confirmed that this had indeed taken place. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to the Security Council report you have mentioned. I am sure it may say what you have said. I don't recall reading it. But the gist of what you have said I recall, because Mr. -- General Spiro Nikovic explained it that the troops, JNA troops, would withdraw from the entire area. That much I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Also, you explained yesterday that an agreement had been reached to observe the provision of the Vance Plan according to which the Territorial Defence would hand over its heavy artillery into the depots under the control of the UNPROFOR and that this indeed took place. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. As regards the objectives of the Vance Plan, and in keeping with the general principles according to which the UNPROFOR mission was supposed to keep peace on the ground, to provide for the negotiations that would lead to the resolution of the Yugoslav crisis and to provide for the return of the displaced persons, with regard to this provision, are you familiar with the fact that in mid-December 1991, the Secretary-General of the United Nations informed the Security Council that he was very concerned about the possibility of a premature recognition of some of the former Yugoslav republics and that he informed about that not only the Security Council but that his envoy also informed about that possibility the members of the European Community? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note the date is mid-December 1991, the relationship to that part of your question where the Secretary-General is informing the United Nations. My answer to you is that -- at that time, I had not joined the mission and wouldn't be in a position to speak to events prior to my joining the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. The timing is clear to me but I put the question to you for a reason that will become clear in due time. With this regard, I would like the Registry to display on the screen Exhibit number 104. This is the report to the Security Council of the United Nations, S 23, 280, dated 11 December 1991. That is the report that I mentioned in my previous question. The reason why I would like to have this document displayed, Mr. Kirudja, is the fact that this report of the Secretary-General considered the conditions for the implementation of the peacekeeping operation in the former Yugoslavia, amongst other things. Have we got the document on the monitor? On the screen? 104. While this is being displayed, Mr. Kirudja, I would like to tell you this: And now on the monitor before you is the report of the Secretary-General of the United Nations. Can we please display the entire first page? Can you scroll up a little, please? In paragraphs 1, 2, 3 and 4, every of these sentences contains in it a provision on the peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia, and now we are going to go to another paragraph that I'm interested in. Can we go to page 8 of the document? And can we zoom in on paragraph 25? In this paragraph, paragraph 25, the Secretary-General of the United Nations informs the Security Council that by the declaration of the European Community from November 1991, a position was put forth that the recognition of individual republics of the former Yugoslavia can be considered only within the overall solution for the former Yugoslavia, and the Secretary-General supports that position. However, in the second third of that paragraph, the Secretary-General put forth his opinion and that was that the proposal for the recognition of those Yugoslav republics that wanted to be recognised contrary to the position that this should be considered within the overall solution of the Yugoslav crisis, might jeopardise the situation, and add fuel to the fire, not only in the former Yugoslavia but in the general area thereof. And in that paragraph, paragraph 25, the Secretary-General informs that on the 10th December 1991, he had sent a letter to the president of the council of ministers of the European Community containing this warning. Can we please go to paragraph 25, to the end of paragraph 25, where this paragraph finishes? Mr. Kirudja, have you been able to follow this paragraph on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Milovancevic? You have written -- you have spoken lines that are almost as long as paragraph 25. We still don't know what your question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I fully endorse the observation of the learned presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all I would like to hear whether Mr. Kirudja has seen the text, has he familiarised himself with the text, and my question is as follows: Does Mr. Kirudja believe that the premature recognition of Croatia and Slovenia that followed this warning indeed worsened the situation in the region and whether the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina created a disaster in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the end of the day? That's my question to Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your learned friend is on her feet but before I let her speak I just want to deal with what I was telling you about. If you want the witness to familiarise himself with the paragraph, stop talking, give him a chance to read. If you are talking, he's listening to what you are saying, he's not reading the paragraph. That's first point. Second point, when you do put a question to him, put one question at a time. Don't put two questions. Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My objection was Mr. Kirudja already answered that he was not there in 1991, he is not familiar with these resolutions which precede his arrival to the area. So I object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the essence of my question was as follows: Some states during the preparations for the peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia actually undermined that operation in the face of the Secretary-General's warning, despite his letter, and actually involved in seeking solution to the Yugoslav crisis outside the framework of the Security Council decision. Mr. Kirudja said that he came in April, that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was peaceful. This question was to be an introduction to my question about the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is the explanation for my question put to Mr. Kirudja, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have to explain your questions. Put your question to the witness. Mr. Kirudja, are you aware of some states undermining the warning of the Secretary-General not to take independence at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I became aware of that when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't need to lay a foundation to that question. Just put the question straight to the witness and the witness will answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, having in mind the fact that you are well familiar with the Vance Plan, you said that upon your arrival you'd heard of the problem of some states being recognised too early. Having had that experience, did you believe it to be so, whether this was only -- the only result was that the situation grew worse in Croatia and in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can testify that the situation in Bosnia soon after our arrival deteriorated in a very rapid manner. I can also answer your question: Yes, we heard all those views inside from mostly Serbs that some states had done what you say they had done. I was in no position, of course, to verify or know what the states did or why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Could we now please have annex 4 put on the screen, of this document, page 21?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm being warned by my colleague that this document was only scanned in nine pages. I didn't know this before. So perhaps we could move on so as not to lose time. With your leave I would move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards your latest answer, Mr. Kirudja, I wanted to hear of your opinion as someone who has worked in international relations for a long time. If the essence of the Vance Plan was to deploy UN troops to secure peace and to find a general solution for the situation, were you able to see for yourself that immediately, after the 6th of April, when Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised, the situation drastically worsened in the republic? I believe you also testified during your examination-in-chief about that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 6th of April, I was still in New York. I didn't -- thereabouts or planning to leave New York. We are talking about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I understand that, Mr. Milovancevic. It is Bosnia-Herzegovina you're referring to when you say the situation deteriorated, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is the 6th of April of which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't really that way when we arrived, at least in the first week of my arrival. Bosnia and Herzegovina was relatively calm, but it might have simply been the calm in the eye of a storm but we wouldn't see it. As a matter of fact we had located our headquarters in Sarajevo to take advantage of the calmness. We didn't see any of the rapid deterioration you are talking about until towards the end of April, when we began to see check-points develop as we travelled in various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. As regards this answer of yours, you mentioned something that was laid out in the basic principles of the Vance Plan, and that was that the headquarters of the United Nations troops was supposed to have been in Banja Luka in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that two departments were supposed to have been located in Belgrade and Zagreb respectively. Do you remember that part of the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With a correction to your statement. The headquarters were supposed to be in three places, Sarajevo for the overall headquarters, and liaison kind of headquarters, one in Belgrade and one in Zagreb. There was not to be a headquarters in Banja Luka. There was supposed to be a logistics base, a military logistics base in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question on this topic of the recognition of individual republics, the Vance Plan contained a provision that the UN troops -- sorry, the JNA troops that were deployed in Croatia, be withdrawn from that territory upon the arrival of the UN troops. Did it seem logical to you, and do you think that the signatories of the Vance Plan, presupposed that those troops of the Croatian territory were simply to cross the republican border to find themselves in their own Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, being able to intervene rapidly from that territory in order to protect the Serbs? Does that strike you as logical?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Difficult question. And I think it makes its point. Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the time of deployment, was supposed to be a peaceful -- there was no issue of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Consequently, there was no issue of Croatian troops going into Bosnia and crossing to attack the Serbs, I assume in the UNPA. The deployment was to be in that part of Croatia where all the four sectors were located, and the achievement implied in your question of protection was to be accomplished by the parties laying down their arms, not the UN coming to fight these people who were armed. The implication was, you lay down your arms, you don't need somebody else from outside to protect you because there is nobody to protect you from if they are not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Your answer is logical, but I had another situation in mind, legally speaking, and factually speaking, in December, January and February of 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina was still a Yugoslav republic. The fact that it was a Yugoslav republic, did it make it easier for the Yugoslav authorities to accept the Vance Plan, because the logic was, as I put it, yes, we will withdraw our troops, they will be in our territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't clear to me that the Vance Plan said where they should go after they have been withdrawn. The JNA was to withdraw all those elements from the areas in Croatia. Maybe I didn't read every line in the plan. I don't think it said where they should go after their withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The last question on this topic: Was it possible to withdraw the JNA troops to the then-Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in your view?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the acceptance of the Vance Plan, you've already touched upon that. You stated that Mr. Milosevic supported the plan. The UN plan. You also stated that Mr. Babic was against the plan, and that he resisted it. Instead of Mr. Babic it was accepted by the assembly president, Mr. Mile Paspalj. Having those facts in mind, did you know that the Yugoslav authorities and the leadership, including the president of Yugoslavia as well as all the other dignitaries, invested a lot of effort to secure the acceptance of the Vance Plan so as to enable the deployment of the UN troops?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clarification for me. When you say president of Yugoslavia, who do you have in mind? It's not Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I had in mind the president of the Presidency. I don't know who it was at the time. I meant the function, not the person. Milosevic was the president of Serbia, one of the people who were important, but I had the entire Yugoslav leadership in mind, when they were accepting the plan.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wouldn't know about the entire Presidency, because you couldn't have the entire Presidency sign an agreement. You can only have particular individuals sign an agreement. You yourself mentioned Mr. Milosevic supported it, and in some subsequent talking with him directly, he seemed to be very active in what happened during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Could we have 65 ter document 227 on the screen? This is a report by Mr. Goulding who was the undersecretary of the SG, dated the 4th?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters failed to catch the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you repeat the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date was the 4th of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since we are waiting for the report, I wanted to go on with the questions, Mr. Kirudja, so as to save time. It contains the notification on Babic's statement, a statement given by the president of the Republika Srpska Krajina, Mr. Milan Babic. This is the document. Could we please go to page 3 of the document? On page 3, you have the translation of Mr. Babic's statement, in which he is communicating to the public and to the UN that the government of Republika Srpska Krajina has not accepted the then plan, on the engagement of UN troops in the Krajina territory, and that the president of the assembly of Republika Srpska Krajina, Mr. Paspalj, did not have the powers to accept such a plan. Can you see that in the text, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm sure you have the same copy I have. Mine is in Cyrillic, and I unfortunately don't read Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Court is in the same kind of misfortune, Mr. Milovancevic, if you can help us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had the English version before me. Pardon me. I wasn't aware that you had the Cyrillic version in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: English version is on the first two pages. The Cyrillic starts at page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right. Thank you, Your Honour. The sequence seems to have been mixed up, from where I'm standing. This is a fax message. Could we please scroll down to the middle?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this text, Mr. Zoran Djordjevic, as a certified translator translated Mr. Babic's position that the government of the SAO Krajina and its assembly were not authorised to accept the plan. Does that tally with the information you had as regards Mr. Babic's conduct at the time, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date I note is February 1992 on this document. Again, it precedes my presence, but all I can say about the document is consistent with my understanding that Mr. Babic opposed this agreement. That was the basis of the Security Council resolution authorising the mission to go on, on the strength of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You saw the first page of the document. That was the fax message sent by Mr. Goulding on the 4th of February and he reported on Mr. Babic's position to the UN. I would like to tender this document, Your Honour, as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence as an exhibit, Defence Exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 766, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see 65 ter document number 231? That is Mr. Babic's letter to His Excellency Mr. Boutros-Ghali, Secretary-General of the UN in York on the 9th of February 1992 by which Mr. Babic notifies Secretary-General that the assembly in Glina that had accepted the Vance Plan did not have the authority to do so, and that the plan consequently is being rejected. I hope that we will have that on the screens soon. The text I have is in English, hence I don't expect any problems. Could we please zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You can see on the top that this is the Office of the President of the SAO Krajina. The letter was sent to the UNSG. At the end of the letter, we see that it was signed by president of the SAO Krajina, Dr. Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Republika Srpska Serbian Krajina, not the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please scroll down to see the bottom of the page? Thank you. Mr. Kirudja, could you please read the middle part, the paragraph that you see beginning on the top of the screen, at the top of the screen?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would like to inform you that the illegal attempt to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kirudja, the next paragraph. It is much shorter. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise too. "Less than one-third of the delegates showed up for the meeting in Glina, which was also attended by General Adzic, acting Minister of Defence, and Mr. Branko Kostic vice-president of the Yugoslav Presidency. According to the constitution of Serbian Krajina, no decision adopted on this meeting has legal power."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please scroll down to the bottom to see the signature block? Drafted and signed by Mr. Milan Babic; is that correct, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding the paragraph you've read out, did you know that Mr. Branko Kostic was the deputy president of the Yugoslav Presidency that Mr. Blagoje Adzic was acting Minister of Defence and Chief of General Staff? Do you remember those names? Do they ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because when I first learned of even the existence of Serbian Krajina republic was in April 1992, when I arrived in Sector North. Prior to that, these documents are all prior to that event of my arrival. But I did know, of course, certain names or hear of certain names like Adzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for our clarification, Mr. Milovancevic, you characterise Brigade Adzic as acting Minister of Defence and chief of General Staff. Minister of Defence of what? Federal Yugoslav Republic or RSK?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. General Adzic was chief of the General Staff of the JNA and acting minister, once General Kadijevic had resigned, and that of Yugoslavia. Mr. Adzic and Mr. Kostic were present at the assembly in Glina, trying to assist the acceptance of the Vance Plan, and in that capacity, they were accused as members of the joint criminal enterprise in their respective indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja, we will now move on to another document. Could we now have the document or rather Exhibit 104? We had it a minute ago on the screens, I believe, the report of the UN Secretary-General, S/23/280. Just before that, Your Honour, I would like to tender this document, the letter by Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The letter by Mr. Babic is admitted into evidence as Defence exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 767, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 5, please, to paragraphs 13 and 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 13, it says that Mr. Goulding informs that at least one of the leaders of the Serbian community does not accept the Vance Plan. And in paragraph 14 at the end of it, in the last sentence -- could you please read it, Mr. Kirudja? The last sentence of paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For the reason described in the preceding paragraph, the assurance sought -- the assurances sought from President Milosevic would be especially important in this regard."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the assurances by President Milosevic, are you aware of the fact that Mr. Milosevic supported the United Nations plan on the deployment of the peacekeeping forces of the United Nations in the former Yugoslavia? Did you know that or did you gain an impression to that effect?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, and I know also directly from him, in discussions I had on the matter with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. As regards the functions that the United Nations troops had in the protected areas, there were three such functions, and in answering the Prosecutor's questions on day 1, you said that there were four war conflicts, and I believe this is the term that you used, but I'm not trying to put words into your mouth. Could you please tell us what conflicts did you have in mind? What attacks were you talking about that were launched against the United Nations protected areas during the UN mandate? I am talking about the three UNPA areas. If I may make things easier for you, on the 21st of June 1992, there was an attack on the Miljevac plateau which was condemned by the Security Council in its resolution 762. Was there also an attack during the Maslenica operation on the 22nd January 1993, which was also condemned by the Security Council in its resolution 802, and was it also the attack on the Medak pocket that was also condemned and you've already spoken about it, and were those attacks on the Western Slavonia, the Operation Flash on the 1st of May 1995, and the attack on Krajina, the Operation Storm, on the 4th of August 1995? Would this be in keeping what you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. You made my answer a little easier by naming the operations themselves. I only make this observation: Yes, I had in mind precisely the first three that you have so correctly listed. There may have been one more that may have been after Medak, but the last two, the ones you are calling operation -- the ones known as Operation Flash and the last one that took over the entire sector, those are not the ones I had in mind because I had by then been reassigned to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. In any case, I suppose that you're aware of the fact that the last two operations also took place?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. In connection to what you have just told us, am I right in saying that the United Nations troops did not fulfil the mission that they were given according to the Vance Plan, which was to prevent any attacks on the territory and protect the population from intimidation? Let me rephrase that and say: Did the United Nations troops, in all of these situations, protect the entire population that still resided in the territories under the UN protection or did they fail to do that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to answer your question and I would like to avoid getting into a debate with you, because the -- I repeat, the UN was not supposed to fight the -- either side, neither the Croats nor the Serbs. In these incidents that you have mentioned, if you go into the details, you will find one or the other or both of the parties in violation of the terms of the Vance Plan, and the resumption of the conflict between the two. In that sense you may be technically correct to say that the UN did not stop the conflict from happening but that would also not be correct to say that the UN was supposed to stop the parties when they violate their terms of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Mr. Kirudja. As regards the five attacks that I have just mentioned, are you aware of the fact that in all the five attacks in these areas under the UN protection, the aggression was launched by the Croatian armed forces? Would that be an indisputable fact in your mind?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be a disputable fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. As regards operation Medak pocket, you provided a supplement to your statement to the OTP, in which you described the behaviour of the Croatian military and political leadership. Do you remember that you said that in your meetings with General Bobetko, the commander of the Croatian army told you, "Tell the Serbs that the long Croatian arm will grab them eventually"? Do you remember that? Do you remember that he told you that even before you sat down and started talking officially?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that testimony is elsewhere. It wasn't obviously adduced in this court but it's also correct that -- what he says, but it wasn't said in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, thank you. I may have not been precise. I did not mean to say that you stated that in the courtroom. I was referring to your statement provided to the OTP. In any case, thank you for the answer. In connection with that answer, in view of the information that you have, would you confirm the position of General Jean Cot who inspected the area of Medak and said that in the villages of Citluk, Pocitelj, and he had not found any human or animal life, that destruction was complete, intentional and systematic? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I characterised that attack in Medak as having been very brutal and shocking to all of us. That much I can say precisely because it occurred in Sector South, where somebody else was performing my functions. And therefore, I couldn't really speak too much to what is -- General Jean Cot had said on Medak. It might very well be correct, what you said, but I can't speak to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the long Croatian arm did get to the Serbs in the Medak area. In connection with this, this intolerant position of Mr. Bobetko, was it only against the Serbs or also against the armed units of the UNPROFOR, for example the Kenyan battalion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting with Mr. Bobetko -- with General Bobetko was about events occurring in Sector North. Yes, you're correct, he just -- what you quoted is what he said, "Go tell them, the long arm of Croatia will reach them." He also confused a number of things, when he was discussing with me, some of which were -- didn't sit very well with me because he made quite a number of accusations about Kenyan troops, not because I'm Kenyan, I'm from Kenya, which I am, it's because the Kenyan troops didn't exist where he thought they existed, and the accusations he made didn't -- were all an imagination, and it wasn't something I took well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would this be a convenient time, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the break, just one more very brief question. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you accuse him of being a racist on that occasion? Do you remember that? Mr. Bobetko, that is.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: His assistants prevented me from telling him what I thought, in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Your Honour, I believe this is the convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We are going to take a break. We will come back at five past 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I might just briefly, during the break we got some information which bears to some extent on the -- our scheduling issue which I just wanted to share with the court so the Court has all the information; also Defence counsel. The flight that the witness had been scheduled to go on tomorrow is at 10 in the morning which is why we were trying to finish today. We learned during the break that there is another flight in the evening at 2100 hours, and so that information may be of relevance. I don't know how -- I, of course, have not spoken to the witness. I don't know what his reaction to that, but I thought I should share that with the Court and Defence counsel so that you have all the information. Perhaps that takes off some of the pressure to finish by today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be okay with you, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm trying to cooperate with the Court as much as I can. It does put a slight strain but I think it doesn't do too much violence in my plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given that answer, then, I suggest -- I suppose what you are saying is that you must still stick to the schedule as we have arranged it and try to see how far we can go and only keep you here as long as it is absolutely necessary tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be appreciated and if we must do it that way, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can tell you if we don't finish with you today you'll have missed the 10.00 flight because we are sitting at quart ore past 2 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, without wasting any time, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. At the very beginning I have already stated my reasons for considering Mr. Kirudja a very valuable witness in these proceedings but we will try to honour Mr. Kirudja's commitments and schedule. Let me proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Kirudja, in commenting Mr. Bobetko's behaviour you said that my -- that your assistants prevented you from telling him "my thoughts." This was what you said. Could you please share with us your thoughts? What would you have said to Mr. Bobetko if you had been given the chance to do so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without going into the details of what he said I would have told him that if we have meetings like this, we are all bound to stick to the facts and it's bad to speak -- to use non-existent facts to make accusations which were basically a slur to a whole group of people, in an official UN meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Bobetko not only displayed an obvious intolerance towards the Serbian side and the Serbs, if somebody says you are going to get caught by long Croatian arms, and asking you to convey that message, he also bragged about the Operation Storm as being his symphony. Are you aware of that? Are you aware of this statement of his?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counselor, Operation Storm took place long after the meeting you are discussing. If he had that in his -- in his mind or up his sleeve, we wouldn't have known it, because at that time he was only talking about implementing the Vance Plan in Sector North and vehemently complaining that it wasn't being done according to the Vance Plan, and because he was by implication, taking us to task for not doing it, therefore he said, "Because you are not doing it the long arm of Croatia will be reaching them."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Just a brief explanation. I believe that you inadvertently you mentioned the Vance-Owen plan and the Vance-Owen plan applied to Bosnia. We are talking only about the Vance Plan. I apologise. This was an interpreters mistake and the interpreter has just corrected herself. You meant the Vance Plan when you were answering my question. I just wanted to avoid that misunderstanding. In regard the operation Medak pocket, do you remember that you carried out a political analysis of the conditions under which it took place? And that your finding was that it took place on the 9 September 1993 and on 12 September 1993 there should have been the signing on the British frigate Avenger on the general cease-fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just supplied me the point I made yesterday. I wish -- I said yesterday I wished I remembered the date on when the Medak took place and thank you for reminding me it took place in September 1993. Yes. It's -- it was in the context at that time 1993, there were many things going on, including what you mention about the cease-fire signing, which I don't quite recall right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In one of the reports, the political circumstances surrounding the attack on Medak pocket was mentioned. It was a UN protected area and the Croatian side attacked it. Political reasons were mentioned and one of the things that was mentioned was the pressure that was put at that time on the UNPROFOR, that the Croatian side demanded radical things. They wanted the Serbs to lay down their weapons, that the Croatian authorities should be restored in the pink zones, and that the mission of the United Nations should be altered. Instead of applying to the entire territory of Yugoslavia, it should have split into the Croatian, Bosnian and Muslim part.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The question is whether this was the case, and whether you remember that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of what you said wasn't even specific to Medak. The Croats had persistently took us to task for implementing both the Vance Plan, with respect to the UNPA, and resolution 762 about pink zones and the restoration of their authority. So you're mentioning that they did demand it was true but it was a constant request from the Croatian side that these things be accomplished. The last part, which is the United Nations mission being altered, I don't recall that it was particularly at this time of Medak but eventually the Croatian side did demand an alteration of the mission, but I'm not sure it was precisely following Medak or a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can 65 ter document 124 be displayed. I have to apologise to my learned friends. I did not expect to use this document but given the witness's answer, I would like to use this 65 ter document. This is a United Nations document, which is relative to the topic that we are discussing at the moment. Can this be displayed? And I hope that it will not be a problem that I have not informed my learned friends about my intention to use the document prior to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There is a report by Mr. Stoltenberg, sent to Mr. Annan. The date is 17 September 1993. The report was from Sector North, the seat in Topusko and the subject is the political aspects of the Medak conflict. I have just been warned that I may have quoted a wrong number when asking for the document to be displayed. Can -- you may be try and trace the document or maybe we can do it later, in order to avoid wasting time. In any case, Mr. Kirudja, do you remember that at the time of the Medak pocket, there was mention of the agreement between the Croatian and the Serbian side on a cease-fire which was about to be signed on the Adriatic Sea on the British frigate called Avenger? Do you remember that? Can you confirm that that is indeed the fact?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this whole Medak pocket conflict, whatever answers I give you, I would like to underscore it took place in Sector South. I wouldn't have followed the details as much as if it had taken place in Sector North where it would be my responsibility to carry both the content of the report and its implications. So I'm surprised that the report you are talking about, about Medak, is from Sector North. Medak was in Sector South. So I wouldn't know all the details you want to talk to me as much as if it had taken place in Sector North. Lastly, of course, I followed the implication of that, and the solution and the -- in broad terms, but I did this not directly, as one responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. I know that you were not directly in charge of the Medak pocket area but I put the question to you, what is something else. The report which I'm not able to locate at the moment. I believe that the number of the document is 886 from the 65 ter list. This report speaks about the political implications of the Medak pocket, arriving at the conclusion that by that operation, the Croatian side prevented any political or military agreements, and in that sense, my question was whether you were aware of that, whether you were aware of that political assessment or not. Maybe you can answer by yes or no, and I apologise once again for tackling a subject that is out of the scope of your sector.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, and I will say you're correct. Strange, this report that you are showing me, I note the first line, a reference to an analysis from me, and I see that the sender of this document, you said, is Mr. Stoltenberg. Actually if you look carefully, it is for Stoltenberg by Cedrik Thornberry, that is in handwriting. Cedrik Thornberry was my direct reporting officer and he would be in a position to receive lots of reports from me, and sometimes you put together an analysis and send it onward to the headquarters. It didn't follow he would refer to me about the analyses themselves, and such was the case with the Medak pocket. He did this. I can honestly say this particular report was never even copied to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at page 8, the last page of this document? It says here that you initialed this document. I'm sure that you were in position to sign quite a lot of documents. In order to avoid any dilemma about the document itself, I'm not checking what you've just told us, Mr. Kirudja, I'm interested in the end of the document. Can you scroll down to paragraph 18, please? Can we go on to the next page? Thank you. Is this your signature, Mr. Kirudja, on this document, or is this your initial?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. This document is written and authored by me. I'm sorry if I -- if my earlier comment gave you the opposite understanding. No, the -- I was only talking about the cover of the document. The document itself, I recognise it comes from me. Its content, it's something I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this document I would kindly ask you, Mr. Kirudja, to read paragraph 13, on page 6 of this document. Paragraph 13, sir. Would you be so kind, Mr. Kirudja, to read paragraph 13 for us?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want it to be out loud?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. "The CA action," CA standing for Croatian army, "the Croatian army action from Gospic into the three villages was preceded by a renewed and virulent attack on UNPROFOR in the Croatian media. Croatian reporters appear to have embarked on a witch hunt for all objectionable things UNPROFOR did or failed to do. The apparent motive was to prop the official demand that UNPROFOR's mandate needed to be fundamentally changed and its command or organisational structure broken up into three High Separate Mission for Croatian, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. In other words, the Croats seem to have embarked in a rather successful media campaign to vilify UNPROFOR and its personnel in the eyes of their own public in an ironic attempt to coerce the mission to act more in line with the official policy for reintegrating the UNPAs back into the rest of Croatia on a fast track. The events that happened in the recent fighting seem to have dealt a severe blow to Croatian official aspirations in this respect."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, does this report conform with what you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for making you read from the screen, which is not always easy. I would kindly ask you to read the next paragraph. It is very brief, and it refers to the British frigate that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Croatian incursion from Gospic into the Medak pocket also happened at the time when both sides were reported to be not too far apart in reaching an accord for a general cease-fire. The negotiating parties were scheduled to meet aboard a British war ship on the Adriatic on 12 September to finalise the agreement. The attack by the Croatian army seems to have pushed the negotiating track to the back burner, if not straight into the ice box. For how long will depend. Perhaps on how the Serbs interpret the positions coming out of the recent fighting. It may be significant that the process to note" -- I'm sorry, "it may be significant in that process to note that the Croatian army in general and Bobetko in particular may have acted in the conviction that the Croatian army action in the Medak pocket would be viewed by the Serbs as an isolated but a potent indicator of Croatian military might to which they could be compelled to respond with a frontal counterattack where the happened. In retrospect, the Croatian army chief of General Staff appears not to have been persuaded that the Serbs --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we finish the sentence, please, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "In retrospect, the Croatian army Chief of General Staff appears not to have persuaded -- been persuaded that the Serbs were poised to respond in full, in total, and everywhere along the confrontation line. Two days ago, he stated to the Croatian press that now the Serbs have felt the long arm of Croatia. It was the same message he had asked us on 7 September to convey to the Serbs. We did."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards this paragraph, Mr. Kirudja, I wanted to go back to one of the answers you provided to the Prosecutor, when you said that the negotiations were on going but they never put into force because they were constantly being obstructed by the Serbs. Does that correspond completely with this, which testifies to the opposite, and that was that the Croatian side interrupted such negotiations, even with such incursions as this one?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counselor, what's the date on this report, my report? Can you please scroll to see the date on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 17th of September 1993, Mr. Kirudja. 1993.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, counselor. My answer is not contradicted in any way by what I read in that paragraph. I mean, my testimony in chief about negotiations being interrupted, because these were many things happening in parallel track. I didn't go into the detail of how those negotiations were conducted, partly in a wish to speed up what the Honourable Judge requested. But if you permit me a second to say what those negotiations were, they were negotiations under Security Council resolution which were characterised as improving economic conditions within the sector and through those economic restoration of relations between the Serbs inside the sector and the Croats, the political process would proceed. But the Croats had put a very strict and significant condition related to the question you ask. They had said, if we had to negotiate about improving economic conditions, we will not negotiate anything that is covered under the Vance Plans and particularly we will not negotiate with anyone in the so-called Serbian Krajina who has a title, meaning government minister. Anyone with an official title and directly related to that government, we will not negotiate. That way, the Serbs in Krajina were forced or asked to name people in their personal capacity who had no titles to continue the negotiations. Those are the negotiations I said the progress in those negotiations was constantly hampered. The people who were involved in that negotiations are almost unheard of here. They had no titles. They were individuals. In this particular instance that we are talking about, this is a breakout of -- or rather an attack conducted by the Croatian army from Gospic into Medak pocket, and this produced very, very significant results of -- in the direction that we have talked about.
