It changed the demobilisation, the weapons storage. Everything changed. This was a military issue, one parallel issue. The other one was a civilian negotiation on a parallel track. What I said is not contradicted, therefore, because of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja for your detailed answer. I wanted to ask you something else as regards those agreements. Did you know that on the 29th of March 1994, the so-called Zagreb agreement was signed, foreseeing the separation of the warring parties and also containing the obligation for the warring parties to withdraw one kilometre away from the line, and that the mortars and tanks be withdrawn ten kilometres in depth, whereas heavy artillery was supposed to have been withdrawn by some 20 kilometres? Have you heard of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you also heard of another agreement that was concluded by the Serb and the Croatian side, much like the first one, with the mediation of the international community in December 1994, concerning economic cooperation; that is, the opening up of a highways, the oil pipelines, and such agreement concerned itself with the stabilisation of the economic situation and cooperation? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I was explaining earlier, and there is a relationship between the two agreements that you just cited. I believe there is a relationship between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, could we say then that these two important agreements were such in which the Serb party has -- had shown goodwill to cooperate? And here I mean to say that it wasn't only the Serb who is have exerted some goodwill but that they were actually one of the parties that contributed to the signing of the agreements?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware those private individuals that I mentioned did carry this agreement to that kind of conclusion you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To move on to another topic, Mr. Kirudja, it concerns the first Croatian attack operation against an UNPA zone, the operation of the Miljevac plateau in June 1992. It was at the time when the UN troops were still being deployed in their respective areas. The Croatian army attacked that area, killed 40 Serb TO members and threw their bodies in a pit and after that, the Security Council put a resolution into force ordering the Croatian side to withdraw its forces from the area. That resolution, 762, and that's why I'm asking you this, concerns another Security Council decision regarding the restoration of the Croatian authority in the so-called pink areas. I believe you would remember that resolution, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your answer given to the Prosecutor, those zones were between the UNPA areas where there were Serbs with their own police, and the cease-fire line. In those areas, there were no Serb policemen. There were supposed to have been no Serb policemen and the Croatian police was supposed to take over those areas. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pink zones?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a 65 ter document number 1360 on the screen? It is a report by the Security Council, or rather to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, what do you want to do with this one that's on the screen, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wish to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is then admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 768, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document and to gain some time, I wanted to say the following, Mr. Kirudja. It seems we have the document before us now. It is number S 24/600.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not get the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The 28th of September 1992. It concerns the implementation of the Vance-Owen plan in Yugoslavia. Since we mentioned the pink zones, could we go to paragraph 25 of the document? Page 8 of the document. I apologise, Your Honours. This paragraph mentions the joint commissions inside the pink zones. According to this paragraph, they were put in place by resolution number 762 from 1992. Such a regime that was foreseen for the pink zones, as foreseen by resolution 762, the implementation of that, did that go without any problems or were there any obstacles to it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many obstacles to that implementation of that resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In view of your answer, yesterday during your testimony in chief, you explained that Mr. Martic agreed with a UN representative on the disbanding of the special police and that the disbanding was resisted by local commanders. Mr. Martic asked that that issue be implemented as agreed with the force commander. Do you remember having given that answer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but that was not implementation of the pink zones. It was implementation of the demobilisation under the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the pink zones, there is a report by Mr. Viktor Andreev, being one of the UN civilian police officers, in which there is a mention, and I'm interpreting, paraphrasing, that the announcement of the re-establishment of Croatian authority in the pink zones will or may become a trigger with the Serb population, causing their reaction. They now want to take the situation in their own hands to do their utmost to make the return of non-Serb populations impossible. This piece of information, does that correspond to what you knew about the problem?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With the view of this answer of yours, could we please have another document put on the screen? We no longer need this document for the time being, although I may yet come back to it. I apologise, Your Honour, I'm thinking on my feet. Could we please see 65 ter document 327? While we are waiting for it, can you recognise the document in front of you, Mr. Kirudja? Could we please scroll down a bit so that we see the entire page? This is a document pertaining to Sector South, not the sector in which you performed your duties, Mr. Kirudja. Why is this document interesting to me and why I wanted to put it to you? It is a report on crimes committed against Croats. Could we please go to the next page? The next page, the third page. I apologise. I was interested in this table. Could we perhaps zoom in or rather see the entire text up to item 29? Thank you. This is a UN civilian police Sector South document. It is a report on crimes committed over a period of time. The first column contains possible crimes, according to their title or name, from one down to 29. In the first line, there is P1, P2, up to P8, and then S 2, 3, 4 and so on and so forth. In order for you to understand what I'm getting at, it is important to note that these markings, P1, P2, and so on are the UN civilian police stations in the pink zone. That's why we have the letter P, and the S 1, 2, 3, et cetera, are the stations in the UNPA zones. In the last column, at the bottom, is there or can you see number 497 of the crimes committed? If we stay with this last digit or figure, and if you go up back to P1, P2, P3, all the way up to S, that is with P8 being the last one I'm interested in, at the bottom we have the total for each of the stations of UN civilian police in the pink zones. Why am I interested in this? The sum total on the crimes committed against the Croats in the pink zones testify to the number of 497, out of which 360 were in the pink zones. When we add up the police stations from 1 to 8, two-thirds of the crimes committed in that period was committed against the Croats, being people or property, in the pink zones. And that figure far exceeds the number of crimes committed in the areas under UN civilian police stations in UNPA zones, from S 1 onwards. This piece of information, that the total number of crimes in the pink zones, that number far exceeds the number of crimes occurring in the same period in the UNPA zones, does that confirm what you've stated just a minute ago, that the inhabitants in those areas, having heard that the Croatian authorities were to be reinstalled, took things in their own hands, trying to prevent or make difficult the return of Croatian population and the re-establishment of Croatian authorities? Does that correspond to what you've just stated? I know my question was a rather long one, but could you conclude that looking at this table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you just look at the screen, that entire screen is covered by the question and beyond. Some of your question has disappeared, Mr. Milovancevic. I don't know how you expect any witness to respond to that kind of statement. You're not asking questions. You're testifying. Why don't you ask questions? Work up to where you want to go by way of questions, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I understand your comment. It seemed to me to be the shortest route, whereas it appeared to be quite the contrary. I didn't want to put each figure, each line and each column to Mr. Kirudja separately but it turned out to be more complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just put one question at a time and build up to where you want to go. You don't expect anybody to answer to all that thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, let's look at station P1. What was the number of crimes there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is there. Just tell him. It is 12. Or 222, if that's what you want. Ask -- ask questions to explain this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't ask him things that are there already, Mr. Milovancevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, if we look at P1, and if we go down to the bottom, the total sum of crimes, is that figure 222? Can you see it there? At the bottom of the table, the first figure to the left, is that 222? And can you see it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. Your Honour, I have a more fundamental problem with this question. This is John McElligott in Sector South, talking about things that happened in Sector South. I was responsible for Sector North. This document is no way shape or form related to anything that came to my office. I can look at a column and quickly add and get 222, if that's what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. I apologise for my previous question and I would like to withdraw it. Let us move on, Your Honours. I understand the gist of your answer, and I believe I have again gone outside the scope of your duties and your sector, of course.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have mentioned the issue of the special police a few questions back, and the issue of the presence of armed people in the field. In one of the answers during your testimony in chief you stated that the Serb TO arms, after the UN troops were deployed, were stored and that after the incursions of the Croatian army, the Serbs took those weapons from the storage and could we relate that to the -- to the Maslenica operation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It began with that Maslenica operation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, you also stated that conditionally put the Serb side, with which you discussed the problem of policemen wearing rifles, carrying rifles, that they were complaining about the need that the police or whatever they were called, and those people carried rifles, had to deal with both crime in general and with the incursions on the part of the Croatian armed forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no incursions of Croatian armed forces into Sector North. The attack in Maslenica that you referred to is far south into Sector South, and way out of the ordinary conflict zone. Maslenica is a bridge. So the thesis you are building doesn't relate directly to Maslenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My intention was not to link this up with Maslenica or with any specific event for that matter. It was a general question. In your discussions with the Serb representatives, when the issue of disarming of the police or the special police was discussed, was the standing answer that the Serbs felt endangered and they needed those weapons and those people to defend themselves? And I have the general situation in mind.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're correct. They did -- they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we again see 65 ter document 1360 on the screen? And this Security Council document, an incursion is mentioned of some 500 to 600 armed Muslims who went through Sector North to reach Bosnia. They were intercepted by the Serb police. Some were killed, some taken prisoner. You mentioned the Muslim prisoners that were detained in the prison in Glina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we go to page 2 of this document, please? Under item D on this page as you're looking from the top of the page, this is it, thank you very much, can you stop there? It says that the prisoners who were interviewed by UNPROFOR said that they had been mobilised and trained by the Croatian army in certain areas in Croatia and were being sent to infiltrate in small groups into Bosnia and Herzegovina, to join in the fighting there. Also, it says that this matter was raised with President Tudjman of Croatia who promised that such practices would no longer be permitted. This created high tensions in the area. Is this information that corresponds to what you know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the group of -- that infiltrated through Sector North, the direction was from the Muslim enclave itself. Outside of the enclave, through Plaski, into Sector North. You're talking about small groups going into Bosnia-Herzegovina, the direction is in reverse. The two issues are not linked in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, does this mean that in addition to this 600-strong group who came from Croatia via Sector North and went to Bosnia, there was another group of Muslims from Bosnia who were trying to pass through Sector North and get to the other side, to Croatia? Is this what you were saying? Did I understand you well? I understand you're talking about two different incidents, two different events?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let's clarify. The group that is referred in paragraph D, the one you have on the screen, stating a large group of armed personnel who were attempting to infiltrate through Sector North into the Bihac Cazin area in Bosnia and Herzegovina were engaged actually even the document in front of you is not accurate. I know the area, I saw that, I went there. They were coming out. They were not going into Bihac. They were coming out of it. They crossed through Plaski. A couple of them were killed and the rest got into Sector North and they were held into Glina prison. I hope that much we are clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that Mr. Martic reached agreement with the UNPROFOR commander on dismantling the special police forces and in your statement to the OTP you explained that General Dukic, but it should be Djukic, came to you, told you that, and that there were local commanders who opposed that but that he had insisted that the agreement signed by Martic should be implemented. Was this agreement actually implemented?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eventually it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to a different topic, Mr. Kirudja. When you talked about your arrival in the area of Sector North, where you were to work, you mentioned who you had met with. You told us that one of your first meetings was with Mr. Lazarevic, a certain Mr. Lazarevic. In connection with that person, I would like to put several questions to you. In your statement given to the OTP, when you mention his name for the first time, you say that you met with Slobodan Lazarevic, the liaison officer of the local Serb government with the UNPROFOR. Later on, when you mention your subsequent meetings with Mr. Lazarevic you say that he was the one who explained to you who was who in the local government and who you should talk to. Your first meeting with Mr. Lazarevic, was it a meeting with a civilian or with somebody wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very first meeting with Lazarevic was in hotel -- in the hotel, the one in Topusko, its name, whatever the hotel, its name is. He was dressed as a civilian, more or less like the attire you find somebody dressed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. At your subsequent meetings with this person, you also mentioned General Spiro Nikovic, the commander of 10th Corps, and you said that you complained to the general about Mr. Lazarevic as the person obstructing the work of the United Nations, and on that occasion, Mr. Nikovic told you that Lazarevic is not in a position to have a say as to who you should employ. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly correct. I wasn't complaining about Mr. Lazarevic because, as yourself observed, if he was a civilian; how come whatever he thought was acted upon? I was complaining about Serb authorities, specifically the police and the police acted in unison, putting this staff member into jeopardy and making demands that the UN staff must be vetted generally, as a general policy, must be vetted by the authorities. Lazarevic was just reporting about that attempt. So the complaint wasn't about Lazarevic, the civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation, Mr. Kirudja. Talking about this Mr. Lazarevic, would this be the person of whom you said that he had sent a message to General Nikovic not to turn up in the territory, Kordun, in the territory of Kordun, because he would be killed and he sent them that message after he was retired? Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same, but it wasn't him sending the message. It is again Lazarevic relying to me, he spoke very good English and partly French, that the authorities are saying, "Tell General Spiro Nikovic, now that he's retired, if he sets foot into our territory, he would be arrested" not killed, arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Lazarevic mention the specific authorities that said that, or he just conveyed the crude message the way you relayed it to us?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He conveyed the message, and it wasn't he himself making the threat. He was making it known to me what the authorities thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this Mr. Lazarevic involved in the arrest of Mrs. Indira Kulenovic, the lady that you testified about and that you mentioned in your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual arrest of Indira Kulenovic was effected by the police chief in Vrginmost, Djuro Skaljac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Lazarevic have anything to do with the arrest? What could you conclude? Did he play a role in that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also spoke about the meeting that you had with a sector commander, or rather the sector commanders and yourself met with Colonel Cedomir Bulat, in a house that was in the vicinity of your base in Topusko. You also said that there were attempts on the part of some RSK officials, together with the Lazarevic as mediator to compromise the first sector commander, and that those attempts were rather obvious. Did Mr. Lazarevic play a role in that as well, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. Again, this is testimony elsewhere, not adduced in this Court, but also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement that you provided to the OTP, did you also explain that this person, Lazarevic, apparently introduced himself to Colonel Bulat with somebody who had a good relationship with representatives of the international community and having represented himself in such a light, he served as an interpreter for Colonel Bulat as well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are we referring to the same Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Kirudja, when you say in your statement that Mr. Lazarevic interpreted in such a way that you had learned from other interpreters that his interpretation was not correct and that this became obvious during the meeting with Mr. Spanovic, when the subject of Medak pocket was on the agenda and that the commander of the sector listened to you and stopped the meeting and disallowed Lazarevic from continuing his interpretation? Is that the Lazarevic that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have another question for you in connection with this Mr. Lazarevic. You describe him in great detail. You say that he was well-groomed, in civilian clothes, that he looked as if he had just stepped out from the step -- from the set of the Great Gatsby. He spoke English very well, he also spoke French, he wore camouflage uniform, and he carried a -- different types of pistol. My impression was that he's the kind of man who could be a very good mercenary. Is that the Lazarevic also known as the Great Gatsby?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the light comment I made but you put them in such a way they are not correct. Individually you may be correct. I met Lazarevic as a civilian very early. Actually he was at the very early meeting saying he was a liaison for European Commission monitors. Progressively he became Mr. -- Colonel Cedo Bulat liaison after the JNA was demobilised. He shifted from wearing these flashy clothes into wearing military fatigues and packing a gun. So the sequence is there but not quite the way -- and I just described the earliest meeting to him because of that flashiness as if in a light comment he would have been in a movie set, and I used the Great Gatsby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I apologise for having put this question to you. I did not mean to put you in an awkward position. You're a decent person. My questions were put in order to get an opinion from you. My question to you is this: You were under the impression that he could have been a good mercenary and that his ideals and life goals changed very quickly and very often. Do you still hold the same view of this person?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you for your kind words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. In answering the Prosecutor's questions, you looked at a document from the 65 ter list, the number is 887. Can we see that document again, please? This is a document dated 10 February 1994, a document which concerns several issues which were topical at the moment. Before we see the document, I would like to ask you something that I forgot to ask you earlier on when we were talking about the acceptance of the Vance Plan. I know that this was before your tour of duty and I apologise for asking you this; however, I would like to know whether you are maybe aware of the following fact. At the assembly in Glina at the beginning of February in 1992, at which the Vance Plan was accepted, Mr. Martic attended and participated very actively in favour of the Vance Plan and in favour of the deployment of the UN troops? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that specific meeting that you mention in Glina, though I don't doubt that it took place as you might have -- as you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Could you please display document 887 from the 65 ter list? This is Exhibit 674, if that may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 764, court Exhibit 764, not 674.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you, 764. It was a slip of the tongue on my part. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Kirudja, is dated 10 February 1994. The document that we should see on the screen any moment now, this is Exhibit 764. I apologise to the Registry for the misinformation. In this document, there is a mention of the topics that were of some interest for you at the time, namely the existence or the introduction of the command for Croatia, General Major Tajide [phoen]. I don't know how to pronounce the name. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately under the title, this document reads, "Message, your liaison officer of the Kordun Corps informed of the position and off the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and under item AAA, can we please scroll down to the bottom of the document to see that item, AAA, and under BBB, there is a mention of the restriction of the movement of CIVPOL, humanitarian organisations, and ECMM, and it says that these restrictions apply to the main roads, that they have to ask permission from the Milicija in advance, and that military conveys are not restrict the. I'm interested in what you say under item BBB of your analysis. Could we please go to page 2 of this document, bearing the marking 732 at the top? I am interested in the middle paragraph, the entire paragraph. In this middle paragraph, you say that with regard the issue of the restrictions on the movement of CIVPOL and the monitoring mission, the authorities in Krajina are divided. In this regard, before I confront you with the entire text, there is mention of the election of Martic as the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. In your response to the Prosecutor's question, you spoke about some ballots and polling stations. You emphasised that you only heard rumours and that you base your statement on rumours. I don't see any link between the ballots and the polling stations and the subject of these proceedings. However, since this question was raised, do you know whether Mr. Martic was elected as president of the republic of Serbian Krajina in the second round of elections? Are you aware of that fact? I apologise, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I was aware that Mr. Martic was elected president. A correction in what I said yesterday. It wasn't rumours. We followed -- I said that we followed the happenings into the sector as they were happening, but on the matter of elections, we had no role in it. It doesn't make it a rumour. It's just that we had no role in it but we followed that an election that was conducted also in Sector North took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I just wanted to see one thing. If you look at the screen, you'll realise that from the top of the screen to just about two-thirds down, you were speaking and your question really came out of the last three sentences after that speech. I just want to you bear in mind, please, just ask your questions, don't give a dissertation before you ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll bear that in mind as much as I possibly can. Sometimes I get carried away by the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that Mr. Martic was elected in the second round of elections are you aware of the fact that in the first round there were seven candidates that in addition to Martic and Babic, there were five more candidates running for president and that none of them gained a majority and that the -- in the second ruined there were Mr. Babic and Mr. Martic the two candidates with the highest vote count in the first round? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the details. Our focus was the last two candidates, which is what the paragraph is speaking about, the last two candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to the Prosecutor's question about this paragraph BBB, your attention was drawn to the last two lines, which say that Martic gained support of Milosevic against Babic and won, and now the question was raised whether he could actually rule or not. My question is as follows: Does it transpire from the text in the paragraph under BBB that Martic was elected as president with Milosevic's support on account of the fact that Milan Babic, as the SDS president, together with the radicals in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, had the majority in the assembly and because they were planning to accuse the UNPROFOR of the lack of efficiency, and based on these false accusations, they were trying to achieve the withdrawal of the UNPROFOR from the Republic of Serbian Krajina? My question is, did Martic support -- did Mr. Milosevic support Martic in order to prevent such a scenario? Is this what this paragraph is about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again, look at what you have said before you put the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And there are two questions, at least more than one question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, if you understand the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The last sentence in this paragraph stems from the fact that he is -- Mr. Martic is elected president with two parties that have an absolute majority of 48 against 34 in the assembly. Secondly, the leader of that group opposing him is Babic, and Babic was always opposed to this mission. The question then, can he govern if he's facing this man with this majority in parliament, that's all the sentence is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your view, and in your opinion, did Mr. Milosevic support Mr. Milan Martic, the accused, in order to prevent Milan Babic from realising his goals and the goal was to chase the UNPROFOR out of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Is that why Mr. Martic gained Milosevic's support, in your view?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes, but I explain it slightly differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you please explain it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explain that many times I know directly from Mr. Milosevic's view later on. Now, when I was in Belgrade, that this is what he wanted. He wanted an outcome that would be consistent with the election of Martic, not consistent with the election -- with Babic. It's that simple. If Babic was elected, then what Milosevic wanted wouldn't have gone through, which is why it says the same thing more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what Milosevic wanted generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He had always -- now I have the benefit of him explaining it to us -- that he always thought that this area should be an autonomous part of Croatia, run by the Serbs, but as an autonomous area, and he was absolutely convinced that President Tudjman may not be able to force a military solution on that part of Krajina. And he said so in many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please see a 65 ter document, number 888?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, I wanted to say that it deals with two topics: Your conversations in Belgrade with Mr. Milosevic regarding Tudjman's refusal to extend the UNPROFOR mandate after the 31st of March 1995, and the other concerning the non-acceptance or the refusal of the Vance Plan. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under the underlined text concerning the subject, there is one sentence and then an entire paragraph. Does one read from that paragraph that the issues discussed are precisely the ones that I just presented to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what paragraph do you want me attention focused on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph after the introductory sentence, the first large paragraph, beginning with, "Yesterday's conference."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what's the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the rest of the text, we see that there is a mention of a conclusion, that being that the Croatian Serbs are following Belgrade's instructions. We will go through the report. Do you remember having mentioned there that Mr. Milosevic was accepting or not accepting the Z-4 plan? On the second page, could we please go to paragraph 3? That is page 2, paragraph 3, after the first sentence, we can read -- or rather I wanted to ask you to read it out for us.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the paragraph with "we assess?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. And after the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We assess that the possibility of Milosevic and Tudjman cutting a deal directly with each other to be more than conjecture. In this light it is perhaps a serious mistake to interpret Milosevic's refusal to meet with the Contact Group as a rejection of the contents of the proposal. It would be more appropriate to see it as Belgrade's tactical move to force the Z-4 group, the legitimacy of which they hardly accepted, to involve Belgrade only in a broader and more decisive forum. A more appropriate forum would allow Milosevic to extract concessions important to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as the price for getting Knin to enter into negotiations on the basis of the Z-4 plan. The question is, therefore, how to serve the peace proposal to the Knin Serbs in a process and form acceptable to Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At that point, would it be convenient? Then you can take up after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a short break. We'll come back at five minutes before 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, regarding the passage you read out before the break, my question is the following: Do you believe that it was wrong to think that Milosevic was going to refuse the ZG [as interpreted] plan for the very reason you've stated, that being that from the start, Milosevic wanted to see the Serbs in Croatia in an autonomous part or state within the framework of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I don't understand that premise. Please restate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase, Mr. Kirudja. The portion of the document you've read out before the break, does that indicate that Milosevic did not oppose the Z-4 plan but, rather, he was trying to come up with a way to involve Yugoslavia as well and to open or get some manoeuvring space with the Croatian Serbs, all that with a view of accepting the Z-4 plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the paragraph actually conveys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement given to the OTP, mentioning Mr. Milosevic, you stated that his position was that no military solution was acceptable, neither for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, nor for Bosnia-Herzegovina, nor for Republika Srpska Krajina. Was that an indication of Milosevic's efforts to deal with the situation in the former Yugoslavia in a peaceful way, through agreement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his most recurrent theme, in almost all the meetings that I had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also stated, in your statement, that Milosevic's position was that if one wants Republika Srpska Krajina to accept the agreement, in order to come up with a peaceful solution, the following things needed to happen. First, the implementation of the cease-fire of March 1992 had to be seen through and respected by both sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic insist on the implementation of the economic agreement as well, on the opening up of the highway and other issues that were meant to improve the political and economic solution, that in turn being conducive to the final, peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not implementation but conclusion of the economic agreement. Not implementation, conclusion of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you also said that you attended many meetings with Mr. Milosevic, and that the circumstances were such that you sat next to him as opposed to Mr. Akashi who was the head of the delegation, who sat opposite to Mr. Milosevic. You also mentioned a question you put to Mr. Milosevic concerning the Serbian constitution, that is the Yugoslav constitution, whether Serbia was the state of the Serbian people. Do you remember having put that question and do you remember the answer given by Mr. Milosevic in turn?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the reason I mentioned the sitting authorities because we were talking informally and because of that accident why I was always asked to sit next and then he would face Mr. Akashi, when the official discussions were over, I would take the opportunity to chat with him about things of interest, and one of them was that question. And I put it to him informally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that an opportunity for you to ask Milosevic something concerning Tudjman's statement that the Croatians had the Croatian state, in which the Serb population complained that they were only a minority and that they were always going to be considered second-rate citizens? Was that a good chance to put that question to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, and it is the question that I put to him, but I also asked him, "Is that the same -- is Serbia a state of Serbs, according to your interpretation of your own Serbian constitution?" That was the question I put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Milosevic answer to your question and, if so, what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He answered it, not only at the time I asked the question but he also answered it for the trial records when I was here and I said, myself, "What did you answer yourself in" and he gave on record the same answer that he gave me the time I first posed the question. And the answer was: This is not the same. Serbian constitution is a secular constitution that was open to all peoples in Serbia. But the rest of what he exactly said I'm sure the counselor can find it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we sum up his question as -- his position being that of condemning such a state as was founded in Croatia and that the Serbian state was the state of all of its citizens and that he was actually proud of his state and Belgrade being the capital of such a state?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression. He took delight in answering that question in the manner you have answered it. He also gave some more details about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As regards this topic, I have another question to ask you, Mr. Kirudja. Mr. Milosevic is no longer among the living. Therefore he cannot confirm or deny any interpretation of yours but I'm interested in your impression, since you were familiar with the events and you knew Mr. Milosevic. Did he ever show any chauvinism or expansionist attitude that would go at the expense of any of the other peoples in the former Yugoslavia? Did you ever hear him say anything of that nature, and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, I can't speak to his relationship with others. I can only speak on my impression of his relations to me, and it was one of courtesy and one of complete ease. When I was with -- around him, he was always courteous and he was also kind of respectful and treated me very correctly in a manner that I remember positively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Without interfering with your cross-examination, Mr. Milovancevic, I just want to say for quite sometime you've been asking about Mr. Milosevic, as if he is the one accused, and I'm not quite sure whether -- or how relevant all these questions are to the case. I just want to remind you that we are dealing here with Mr. Martic's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very relevant, Your Honour, because the indictment accuses Mr. Martic of being one of the creation of the plan on joint criminal enterprise, together with Mr. Milosevic and others, in order to expel all non-Serbs -- non-Serb populations from large territories in Croatia and Bosnia, in order to create a unified Serb state. That is what the relevance of my previous question was, and with your leave, I wanted to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, did he ever, in your presence, Mr. Milosevic, I mean, as the alleged leader of the plan, did he ever mention or even gave or hinted at his intent or wish to expel or kill members of other peoples in order to create a unified state?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no context for that to come up, or even be discussed, so my merely saying no, it also says we discussed something like that. No, there was no context for that kind of question to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With a view of your last answer, when you met Mr. Martic, were you given the impression that Mr. Martic wanted to expel or destroy any other peoples or to mistreat them in any way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The few times Mr. Martic and I met, I never heard anything like that, but then again, we didn't talk a lot with Mr. Martic. Mr. Martic always struck me as the quiet type in these meetings. He didn't speak too much, at least in the meetings that I met him with -- in -- met with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With that in mind I wanted to remind you of a portion of your statement pertaining to the Bihac pocket situation and your conversations with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Martic on the need to let the humanitarian assistance go through. Did Mr. Martic support the intention of yourself and Mr. Akashi to send that aid to the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not at first. He had to be talked into that by Mr. Milosevic himself. As I recall, Mr. Martic himself, on one of the few occasions when I saw him worked up he was quite worked up about that and at first he didn't even want humanitarian assistance to go into that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was somewhat unclear. Actually I wanted to know whether Mr. Milosevic supported your position and that of Mr. Akashi. Maybe I misspoke. Your plans concerning the sending of the humanitarian aid and did he offer his assistance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That humanitarian aid was supposed to have been received by the Muslim population, if I understood that correctly. It was going to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your view, such an attitude by Mr. Milosevic, did that testify as to his attitude towards the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic's attitude? Or Mr. Martic's attitude?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. I have Mr. Milosevic in mind.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic spoke on that issue from his full understanding of the international requirement and specifically international humanitarian law, not to use humanitarian assistance against any group of people, and he spoke from that context to say to Mr. Martic, "You can not impede the humanitarian assistance into this pocket." That's the context he spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the Bihac pocket, and the so-called Cazin region, I have several questions. The Bihac pocket or the Cazin Krajina, adjacent to Sector North, was that in between the Serb areas where UN troops were deployed as well as some other Serb-held territories in the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the pocket comprises several municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the leader, so to say, of the Cazina region or the Bihac pocket a person by the name of Fikret Abdic? He was a Muslim leader.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, leader? Rather it's more correct to say that he was an extremely influential person based in that pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. When I used the term "leader," I had the status such as you described in mind. Is it correct that Mr. Fikret Abdic, being a Muslim, was for the way to resolve the situation between the ethnicities in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a peaceful way as opposed to Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I met with him also many times both in his own private house as well as his house. I have heard his views and he also expressed that a peaceful solution in Bihac -- Bosnia-Herzegovina was the way to go, and he thought he knew the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that his views clashed with those of Mr. Izetbegovic? And could you tell us what it was that Mr. Izetbegovic wanted as opposed to Mr. Abdic's attitude?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counselor, perhaps you should go the other way. I know what Mr. Abdic wanted but not what Izetbegovic wanted since I never met with Izetbegovic. But I have met with Mr. Abdic. Abdic had gone to the extent of creating what he called Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, meaning creating a prototype in that pocket area of a regime, a state like you wanted to see happen everywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that agreement he had co-signed by Mr. Milosevic himself, Mr. Tudjman, and himself, and that was what he wanted to model the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina to look like. It didn't fit with what they were thinking in Sarajevo and not long after, he, Mr. Fikret Abdic, ended up being in a conflict between one portion of that pocket, which he controlled from his base in Velika Kladusa, and the military command controlled by Sarajevo, which was based in Bihac. And he lost that conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The agreement signed by Abdic with Milosevic on the 22nd of October 1993, did it also foresee the mutual recognition of the western Bosnian region and the Serbian Krajina? Was it also supposed to put peace into force between the western Bosnia area and the rest of the Serb-held territories in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: And Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the intention. Fikret Abdic wasn't too sure that he can bring together both the Serbs, Muslims and Croats, and he was going to use Western Bosnia, what we are calling Bihac pocket, as a prototype to show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with one of our earlier answers, let me ask you this: Such a behaviour by Abdic, who was in favour of peaceful solutions, did this result in the attack of the 5th Corps of the army under the command of Dudak against Western Bosnia and the defeat of Western Bosnia? Was this the reason for the attack of Dudakovic's corps against this Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall Dudakovic attacking Krajina. As I recall, it was the opposite. It is Abdic using his forces, enlisting the forces in the Serbian Krajina to join with him to attack the rest of Bihac pocket. It's the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that Fikret Abdic sought assistance from the Serbs from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and that they extended that assistance? In other words, they responded to his application? Is that what you're saying? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that at the end, the 5th corps of Alija Izetbegovic's army defeated Abdic's forces?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that earlier. He was defeated and he was defeated by the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The 5th Corps of the BiH army, did it also attack the Serb side? Did it cross over to the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Do you know anything of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Serb forces from Sector North started shelling into the Bihac pocket, they responded, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you are talking about the Serbian shelling, this was at the request of Abdic's side; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to this situation in the Bihac pocket, you mentioned a meeting in Belgrade with Milosevic and Martic. This was during the shelling of the Udbina airport by NATO, and you also told us that at the time, Martic at one point opposed to the delivery of the humanitarian aid, although Milosevic had pressured him into accepting that and not be opposed to that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another topic. Mr. Kirudja, you've mentioned the year 1992 and the murder of Mr. Obradovic, one of the mayors in your sector. Was it ever established who the perpetrator of that murder was, who killed this man?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, and I had more reason to find out whether it was solved, it wasn't until the time I left my posting in Belgrade. And even when I was in Belgrade, I was in touch with some of my previous colleagues and counterparts and had occasion to ask if the murder had been solved. It was -- nobody would even dare to talk about it. Many -- about two or three years, not two or three years, about a year or so after the fact. I said I had a reason to do that because I had known Obradovic and I had known his family and from that point, and I knew them well, humanly speaking I wanted to know if they had got his killers. And I never got to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that as soon as the killing of Mr. Obradovic became known, the president of the assembly of the Serbian Krajina, Mr. Mile Paspalj came to the scene. He belonged to the government in where Martic was also won of the ministers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that -- actually you provided us with a possible conclusion, that the initiative or a suspicion was cast also on the government in Knin, as a result of the pressure on those measures. My question to you is this: Are you aware of the fact that the indictment charges Mr. Martic with the participation in corridor when Mr. Obradovic was killed? According to the indictment, Mr. Martic was on the corridor. Are you aware of this detail?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what do you mean in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the operation that was conducted in July 1992 in order to liberate the road that had been intercepted or blocked by the Croatians in the northern part of Bosnia. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now that we are talking about Mr. Obradovic, does the fact that a high official of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Mile Paspalj, the president of the assembly, came to the scene after the killing of Mr. Obradovic in a state of shock and, under the arms, like everybody else, does this fact point to the fact that the Knin government did not have anything to do with the killing or else, the way you put it? And you're an experienced person, able of assessing the situation properly. What is your view of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't conclude that. Mr. Paspalj was obviously, along with others, quite, not just shocked. There it was an element of fear around. That's why he carried a gun, I mentioned. I had never seen him carry a gun before. And it wasn't the scene that he came to. He came to the hospital, where they were trying to save Mr. Obradovic. The surgery was going on. The conversation that took place at that point indicated that apprehension and fear of not knowing who was responsible and whether it could happen to anybody else. That was the point. Secondly, a major--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Anybody else, including himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When you don't know, you don't know. So I took it that's the reason he's carrying a gun, to protect himself. Then there was the situation of where it happened. As I said, in a small place, two kilometres, forest, at the corner there it was the headquarters of Cedo Bulat, a military headquarters n front of the road there is a check-point of military. There was no way a stranger even would get away with that kind of a crime, in my view, in such open way, in the morning, around 9.00. So whoever committed this crime, the very least is somebody in authorities let him get away with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why would somebody let the perpetrator get away with it? Serbian authority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my question that I wanted to know. Why? Because he's a mayor, he's an authority like everybody else. This route was a regular route. His house was not very far from there. And at that time, I also recall there was this understanding that some mayors had certain views. I spoke about it yesterday. And he was one of those who kept to himself and did things according to the Vance way, not the current way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these police who were guarding that road around there belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbian Krajina. Armed, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And he was shot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in broad daylight. 9.00 in the morning, around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this answer, I have two more questions. Mr. Mile Paspalj, on the day when this happened, was the president of the assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and there is no dispute about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And since Mile Paspalj signed the acceptance of the Vance Plan on behalf of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was actively supported by Mr. Martic, could you exclude the possibility that, for example, Mr. Babic had some interest in committing an act of that sort or some of his sympathisers, who were against the Vance Plan? Could you exclude that possibility?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seems to me far-fetched. Babic was in Knin. Babic himself at times was a victim of attacks. At one time he was hospitalised, had occasion to talk to Babic many times. Babic himself had an element of fear going around. He was not part of the authorities himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with your last answer, are you aware of the fact that there was an order for Mr. Babic and his family to be executed and this order was issued by the Croatian authorities? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware. I just said that I'm aware he was attacked and hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another topic, Mr. Kirudja. Let's talk about the transport of the Muslim population from Bosanski Novi, and you spoke about the obvious cooperation between the mayor of Dvor and the mayor of Bosanski Novi. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The period is June and July 1992. Was that the time when, in that area, or at least in the territory of Sector North and on the entire territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, there were a lot of problems with supplies, with food stuff, with electricity, water and the likes? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, or do you know, better say, that the Operation Corridor took place after the Croatian side had cut that corridor in two and when the situation for the Serb population had become even worse? Do you remember that, there was no way of delivering anything by air or by road?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Serbian population do you have in mind? Both in Serbian Krajina or in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in both?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I meant -- I meant the Serbian population in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, in UNPA zones?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the only supply route for those Serbs who were in the UNPA. There was also a supply route coming from Karlovac to the crossing point in Turanj and there was much less used supply route through Sisak. We had a lot of supplies coming in, either as humanitarian assistance, and Fikret Abdic of which we spoke about just a few minutes ago, had a whole convoy of trucks that he would arrange coming in through Karlovac into the pocket with the full arrangement of the Krajina Serbs themselves. So the corridor you're talking about which goes through Bosnia-Herzegovina to Belgrade was not the only one that would have supplied the Serbs in the UNPA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Karlovac, which is to the north of Sector North, was a town under the Croatian control, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During the Operation Corridor, did you hear of the death of 12 babies in the hospital in Banja Luka due to a lack of oxygen which could not have been transported from Belgrade, all that as a result of the problems that I have just spoken about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, but I also conceded to you that the Serbs in Bihac needed the corridor. I was only specifically talking about the Serbs in the UNPA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In light of all the economic hardship, do you think that the interest of the authorities, for example, in Dvor, which is across from Bosanski Novi, not to keep four, five or 6.000 refugees in their territory is the result of nationalism or that it may have had something to do with the problems in the supply and the way these people could have been provided for?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Question to you: 6.000 refugees, are you -- in Bosanski Novi, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no 6.000 refugees in Bosanski Novi. People are not refugees when they are in their own houses. Even if they be Muslims, which they were. They were in their own homes. They can't be refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this answer, let me ask you this: Do you remember a conversation with Mr. Martic which took place on the 10th of May 1995, in Belgrade, the conversation between Martic and Mr. Akashi after the Operation Flash, Mr. Akashi was in favour of the position that the Serbian population should leave Sector West. In your view, was that a voluntary departure or was that a necessity and in view of helping these people save themselves?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sector West, the Serbs who were there after Operation Flash, I assume you mean after the Croats took the action they took, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if your question is, was it a voluntary move, I don't think so, that the Serbs didn't wish to be in that place when the Croats came in. Now, that is important because the Serbs and the Croats had engaged in a conflict that even preceded our arrival. The Croats, a lot of people were -- who were Croats were pushed out of Sector West, which you are describing, and I started there in Daruvar. I went to Pakrac and I went to other areas. Therefore, this fear of the Serbs was of retaliation if the Croats came in, and that is understandable, that they wouldn't want to be there for fear of retaliation. Now back to Bosanski Novi, if that's the analogy you're trying to draw, there was no such cycle of these people you're calling 6.000 refugees. These were people in their own houses. The Serbs declare: We have a new Srpska republic and you have to swear allegiance to it. Those are two different scenarios.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with your last answer, Mr. Kirudja, do you remember that you had conversations with the Muslim representatives of the municipalities and towns who wanted to leave and that an explanation was provided that people had relatives abroad, that they wanted to escape the situation at hand? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two representatives of the Muslims who were brought by a group of Serbs so that they can explain to me how come the people wanted to leave, yes. To leave Bosanski Novi. We are talking about Bosanski Novi now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In those conversations that you had, Mr. Kirudja, the Serbian representatives told you, is it correct or not, that the Muslims did not want to go to the territory under the control of Alija Izetbegovic because they would be mobilised, they didn't want to fight, they wanted to go abroad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the Serbian representative said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can my last document of the day be shown? That is a document from the 65 ter list, 1829.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the previous document, is it already in evidence or you don't need it in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would apply for the admission of this document as a Defence Exhibit. If my learned friend from the Prosecution has used this document, then it will soon be known, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I didn't use it so it is your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, can this be admitted as a Defence Exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is then admitted as a Defence Exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 769, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. All right. Now, what document did you want called, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last document that I'm going to show, Your Honour, and I'm drawing my cross-examination to an end. This is document 1825, 65 ter list document 1829.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology, 1829.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, this is a Prosecutor's document speaking about the first carriages of Bosnian refugees to Germany. The date is 26 July 1992. Can you see that on your screen? Can you please read out the first line below the word "body"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the line reads, "Three trains carrying some 2.600 distraught and exhausted Bosnian refugees fanned out across Germany on Sunday, as Bonn put on an emergency relief drive for civil war victims into action."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the next page of the same document, bearing the digits 259? Below the page number 36, the Reuters library report July 26, 1992, could you please read out the three last sentences on that page? Can we please scroll up to display the bottom of the page? Not the last page but the three -- not the last sentence but the three sentences but last and I promise you this is the last thing that you're going to be asked to read out today.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confused. The last -- beginning with Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The refugees, starting with the refugees. The fourth paragraph from the bottom would be the beginning of what I'm asking you to read. Starting with the words, "The refugees came."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. "'The refugees came mostly in families, many with children, and the first train also had a surprisingly high number of young men on board,' Red Cross Dr. Hans Plasche [phoen] said."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the next two paragraphs as well, and my question will be forthcoming after that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Plasche said a colleague had reported Croatia was letting Bosnian men leave rather than force them to return to fight. Most refugees seemed in good health, although several children were sunburned and many were dehydrated after waiting hours in the sun for evacuation from Karlovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Karlovac is a place in Croatia, and the Croatian government had agreed that it should be used as a starting point for the transportation of this Muslim population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you pull up this -- the date on this report, please? I don't see the date on it. July 26, sorry. Thank you. This must only have a reference, if the reporting is correct, to the number -- the first time we evacuated the 4.000 from Bosanski Novi, or it -- if it doesn't refer to that group, it could only refer to smaller groups we spoke yesterday that came and went past the -- past the sector. In most cases, one of the biggest headaches I had was if a convoy of Muslims contained men, if there were men in the convoy, the Serbian police and military went into high gear, demanding that they should be pulled out and therefore I can't relate over this issue about them refusing to go back and fight, because the reality was most of the people who passed through that sector, around 26 of July, as this document is dated, were mostly women and children. If there were men, we had a lot of trouble with the Serbian people letting them across the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The three paragraphs that you have just read out, do they speak about a surprising number of young men among the refugees? Does the report say that the Croatian side had allowed Bosniak males to leave rather than to return them in to fight? Is this what it says in this text?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm having a lot of trouble commenting on a journalist's story. Often journalists are not the kind of places you go for accuracy in everything. This is a Reuters story. I explained to you about the daily events in the sector. It's hard for me to believe that they were talking about a lot of men coming from Bihac pocket through the sector into Karlovac. On the other hand, I knew for a fact there were a lot of men already prepositioned in Karlovac that I had met at their request because they wanted to talk to me about it and they were already there in Karlovac. So this story about men, unless you knew the genesis of it, you don't know whether they were already in Karlovac, you don't know whether they transitioned through the sector. It's difficult to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And one more question about the convoy carrying 4.000 Muslim refugees from Bosanski Novi: Was this convoy organised by the UNPROFOR and the UNHCR? Did it enjoy all the logistical support by these two organisations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not correct that it was organised by UNPROFOR and UNHCR. It was organised by the Serbs centred around Bosanski Novi, in the mayor's office, Pasic, and Dvor's office, over there. But because they were going to transition through the sector, then obviously we were involved, if only for humanitarian reasons, in helping them out to complete this transition. I testified yesterday the police -- the Serbian police were out in force managing it. We read a memorandum yesterday showing the buses were all provided for by the Serbs. It was not organised by UNPROFOR or UNHCR in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more thing about your observations: There is a report of yours, an UNHCR report talking about the vicious circle in the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in which the Serbs wage war against the Muslims, the Muslims against the Serbs, the Croats against both, and so on and so on, and all this is an endless cycle of crimes committed against the innocent population. Was that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: An UNHCR report is not technically my report in the first place, and I am not sure exactly the specific one that you are referring to. That's one point. And as to a vicious cycle in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is truth to that in the very broad sense. One act begot another, and in the very broadest of sense, yes, there was a vicious cycle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But is it true that in any case, even if the report had been yours, at the time of writing it, you would have believed it to be true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That there was a cycle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whatever you wrote in the report you believed that to be true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I would like to thank you for all your answers. We don't have any more questions for you. The cross-examination lasted as long as it did because of the coverage, both in terms of time and space. I hope that my cross-examination was not too tiring, given my attempt to provide a somewhat lengthy introduction into every topic that we discussed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Ms. Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There won't be any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova. Judge? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kirudja, may I ask you some questions? First, we saw a report of Mr. McElligott about crime figures in Sector South. It brings me to the general question, how your position related to Mr. McElligott's. How can this be compared with your function with regard to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe the exact title of John McElligott was Deputy Commissioner of Police, in the report that you cite. Each -- we were organised with that respect along the following lines. The civilian -- the United Nations civil poll, civil police, were deployed in each sector. Every opstina reasonably close to the Serbian police and sometimes other places, we had a deployment of civilian police in the sector. Those civilian police reported to a chief of police who was in my office. In Zagreb, there was a commissioner of police who coordinated all that work, because there were similar arrangements in the other three sectors. John McElligott was in Zagreb later, and I believe he might have been also in Knin for a short time in Sector South but he would have been the person in Zagreb who would be at the receiving end of the reports coming from all sectors on behalf of his boss, the commissioner, but in my sector, there was somebody else, he was in directly linking called the chief of police.
