Not McElligott, there was a chief of police in each of the four sectors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And how about three other UN persons, and their technical relationship to your function. Mr. Thornberry first.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry was the head of civil affairs. This was very carefully calculated role that Mr. Goulding had created, Marek Goulding being at that time the Undersecretary General for the entire peacekeeping. It was consistent with something we have discussed here at length, that UNPROFOR did not have a mandate to sort out political problems. Therefore, the United Nations had appointed as head of the mission rather unusually a soldier, the force commander. Force commander at the beginning was the head of the mission. But because he was a soldier, he couldn't be expected to deal with other non-military matters. That responsibility was placed under the head of civil affairs, and that was the role Cedric Thornberry played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And finally two persons, Mr. Akashi, the Secretary-General's special representative to the former Yugoslavia, how did he relate to UNPROFOR? And to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I just described, that setup lasted only for one year, because it became clear, as the deterioration of events that we spoke of in Bosnia-Herzegovina became evident, the United Nations management Secretary-General decided to return to the normal structure of a UN mission. It wouldn't be headed by a soldier. It has to be headed by a civilian. And the first civilian that headed UNPROFOR was Stoltenberg. Mr. Stoltenberg also had the other responsibility of being a co-chairperson of the international conference in the former Yugoslavia for the UN. Lord Owen for the European Union. Mr. Stoltenberg didn't want to keep that role for long. He lasted almost another year. And by the end of 1993, that is when Akashi replaced Mr. Stoltenberg in the title role of special representative of the Secretary-General. In that case, he took over the leadership of the mission and the force commander reported to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And what was then the function of Mr. de Mello who also appeared in one report together with the name Akashi? Can you give me a just short --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A short one. When Cedric Thornberry ended his tour in his role, because he continued to be head of civil affairs, he was replaced by de Mello.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, after these technical questions, as to the implementation of the Vance Plan, you said, Mr. Kirudja, the Vance Plan included that all armed elements would lay down their arms. Yesterday you explained us a document containing a list. This is court Exhibit 748 -- of, first, it was said, JNA units stationed in Sector North, and below, the second list, weapons left behind by JNA. From infantry weapons to tanks. Acknowledge you explained to us that they were taken into custody of UNPROFOR with this two-key system. This process took place at the end of May 1992. But how complete was, this in your view today, this demilitarisation, beside the issue you discussed yesterday, the turning back of certain arms to Serbs, in order to counterbalance for a possible Croat attack? You pointed out that not all arms had been turned in for storage. But you then left from that issue of arms remaining in Serb hands in the sector by pointing to the easy possibility to import arms from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, what to your impression, was the amount of arms which had remained in the sector but not were turned in at all?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The last question quite simply I couldn't quantify them and tell you so many. I also have to clarify that my impression is that at the end of May, when we took possession of those arms listed in the exhibit, my impression of that, we took pretty much all of them that were of -- turned in, because it was a voluntary exercise. Troubled and difficult but nevertheless the voluntary exercise where the Serbs turned these weapons. By that I mean they didn't have a lot of reason to hide lots of them from us. I also testified that by the end of the year, when the Maslenica operation took place, they went and demanded and took out those weapons, fearing further attack by the Croats. The implication was that those weapons were never returned, ever after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You said that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And thirdly, in between the time when they were in storage and when the operation took place and they reclaimed the weapons, there was a progression where they built up a parallel force with long weapons. We also talked about that. And those had weapons. And when you ask me where did they get them from I can't say we gave them from the storage, because we didn't. So I assume they got them from elsewhere. And it wouldn't have been difficult for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But they more or less were apparently imported brought from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifications. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I have just one question now. Actually two by reason of the fact that Judge Hoepfel has covered some of what I had to ask you in his first three or so questions. But what I want to ask you touches and concerns the Vance Plan and the implementation of it. Did the plan as agreed encompass any direction to your mission UNPROFOR as to how to deal with violations by any of the parties of the terms of the plan? And if yes, were these terms implemented? For example, when there was a violation, what would happen on your side? How would it be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Times have changed since the UN was doing that mission. The practice then was, if the Security Council issued you with a mandate as UN, and any part of that mandate was violated, you reported it to the Security Council as a violation of a Security Council mandate and it was up to the Security Council to take whatever action that was necessary. And in answer to your question, there were many violations, and some of the reports reported back to the Security Council that there were violations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have cancelled quite a number of my questions because the Judges have already asked them. You testified today sometime that the Serb side showed cold feet towards a certain agreement. My question to you is: How did they demonstrate the cold feet? What made you say this is now cold feet?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very protracted process, Your Honour, involving these private individuals I explained today where we would sit down and talk about various aspects of bringing economic normalisation, and at the beginning, you didn't know whether you reach a conclusion or not, but you went on. We knew at certain point we were reaching a consensus because we are in the room, we are talking to different parties the parties were negotiating in my presence and I know how far progress they have made. Until when we knew that certain progress was coming, the Croats now were interested in changing the formula slightly to allow those who were in authority in Knin to come in at that point when agreement was coming together. It stands to reason, private individuals couldn't sign an agreement, so when the Knin authorities were approached in one case to go into a meeting where we knew the offer was to be put on the table and we knew they knew them, they cancelled. They cancelled the meeting in media. At that time, the plane was in the air when we were told they are not coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've already answered the next question I was going to ask. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also testified today about this testimony that the long arm of Croatian -- the long Croatian arm will grab them eventually and you said that testimony was not given in this court, it was given elsewhere. Where was it given?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to be in the trial of Milosevic himself. I'm not quite sure, because the document that counsel was quoting has that testimony and it is the document that was submitted in full and in extenso in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Relating to the killing of Mayor Obradovic, now, I know very little about investigations and I'm just asking you here. You said he was shot at. There could have been cartridges left on the scene. It would have been the simplest thing to pick them up for forensic tests and find out from which guns they came. Sorry I see you keep nodding. I would like you to speak because we won't see your nod on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was waiting for you to finish and I'll take the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The question really is that way the perpetrator could have been easily identified.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, when the assassination occurred and I was notified about it, I went past where the vehicle was. I saw it in that position, still shot, and all the scene of the crime was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fresh with all the --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fresh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: With the cartridges.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was there violent as it was but I had much more important thing to get to the hospital where he was being operated because the issue of evacuation, medical evacuation was prominent. And as I said, there were police everywhere, Serbian police. To today's date I never heard that they apprehended anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's the last of my questions. Ms. Richterova, any questions arising from the questions of the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic? Further cross-examination by Mr. Milovancevic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning Judge Hoepfel's question concerning the weapons in the territory, Mr. Kirudja, did you know that at the time there was a resolution of the Security Council in place on the prohibition of importing of weapons in the territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure the resolution was in the entire Yugoslavia. There was a resolution restricting weapons in Bosnia-Herzegovina and there was a -- sanctioned in Serbia and Montenegro. I don't think it was overall but I could be wrong on that. I don't recall an overall for the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia, primarily because it wouldn't have applied to Slovenia, it wouldn't have applied to the rest of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the remaining part of Croatia could arm themselves any which way they wanted and they were indeed quite well armed, is that correct, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Croatia was quite well armed and continued to build their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question concerning Mr. Obradovic. You said that he was assassinated on a forest road, some two kilometres into the forest, if I understood properly. Can you assess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say assassinated or killed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I have not used those two terms intermittently, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is the same thing in my view he was ambushed, his vehicle was riddled with bullets. He was killed, assassinated. In any case the man was dead. That was in the forest or rather on a forest road some two kilometres into the forest self f I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not two kilometres into the forest but two kilometres from my office, almost, but in a wooded area that you passed through to get in and out of Topusko itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: One last question: This forested area, since it was wartime, was it simple or difficult to control such an area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counselor, don't get the idea that it was a forbidding forest area, it's particularly wooded, there are settlements in there the command of Cedo Bulat was in behind the forest and we were just in front where you come tout of the forest, that's where our head quarters was -- there was a hotel there. It is into the foreboding a forest. But it was a very convenient place to lay an ambush for such an ambush is what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The last question: If you know, what was the percentage of all crimes and perpetrators of -- thereof that are discovered in the world -- in countries of the civilised world, in particular the western world? Are you familiar with such figures?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does it come from the questions from the Bench? Any way, you have been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Kirudja, thank you so much. This brings us to the end of your testimony. You will catch your 10.00 flight tomorrow. We thank you very much for accommodating the Chamber and also for the testimony you gave. You are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Travel well back home. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf the Prosecution if I could just express my thanks to Your Honours and to Defence counsel and most particularly to all of the staff, the interpreters, the Court reporter, the AV people for sitting the extra time today. We are extremely grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. You just took the words out of my mouth. I was waiting for the witness to get out of the courtroom before I thanked everybody for their accommodation and their enthusiasm with which you really helped us. It's not only helping the Prosecution, it's helping the entire process, and the Chamber does appreciate your help in that regard. I'm not singling anybody out. Everybody, Defence, technical staff, the witness, the interpreters, everybody, including registry and the other judges. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: We thank you also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a piece of information. I still owe you an answer. You asked the witness where the statement was from. Perhaps it is somewhat late but I wanted to state it nevertheless. The statement you mentioned was the statement provided by Mr. Kirudja to the OTP in September 2001. You asked him what the statement was from which he referred to the incident with Mr. Bobetko. I didn't have the time to share that with Mr. Kirudja but I wanted to share it with you having received that piece of information at this moment, somewhat belatedly, and I apologise for that but I thought it might be interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm actually a bit lost. I'm not quite sure I understand what you're talking about but that's fine. Thanks for all the help. It is late in the day. We will adjourn and convene tomorrow again at quarter past 2.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
